headline: Cannabis research: CBD nasal dosing cut sinus inflammation in mice
dek: Three new lab and animal studies test CBD for sinus inflammation, hemp seed in yogurt and cannabinoids in mouthwash. None has been tested in people yet.
key_points: A University of Toronto study in mice found intranasal CBD cut a key marker of chronic sinus inflammation by about 41% against a control, with no side effects observed.
Spanish researchers reported in Molecules that yogurt made with treated hemp seed had more protein, more polyunsaturated fat and stronger antioxidant activity.
Thai researchers found a full-spectrum hemp mouthwash reduced bacterial activity on enamel samples by about 56%, though chlorhexidine was the stronger antibacterial.
All three are early-stage studies: one in animals and two in the laboratory, so none shows a benefit in people.
body: Three studies reported this week look at cannabis and hemp outside the usual focus on THC: a CBD solution for chronic sinus inflammation, hemp seed as a yogurt ingredient, and a cannabinoid mouthwash for dental bacteria. All three come from early-stage research, one in mice and two in the laboratory, and each is a first step rather than evidence that a product works in people.
We read the summaries published by The Marijuana Herald and link the journal records below. Where a figure comes from the Herald's account rather than the paper, we say so.

Researchers at the University of Toronto tested intranasal CBD in mice with experimentally induced chronic rhinosinusitis, a long-lasting inflammation of the sinuses, according to the Herald's account of the study in the Journal of Otolaryngology – Head & Neck Surgery. The study used 55 mice: 50 with the condition and five healthy controls. Animals received one of two CBD concentrations, a control solution, or mometasone, a corticosteroid used to treat the condition, three times a week for three weeks.

The higher CBD concentration reduced the activity of eosinophils, a type of inflammatory white blood cell, by about 41% compared with the control. Both concentrations reduced abnormal thickening of the nasal lining, and the lower one also reduced abnormal protein deposits. On eosinophil activity, the researchers found no statistically significant difference between high-dose CBD and mometasone, though the steroid did better on some structural tissue changes. The team reported no CBD-related adverse events, weight changes or blood abnormalities. The Herald notes that the condition affects up to 12% of people, and that human trials are needed.
Evidence level: animal study. It suggests a direction for research, not a treatment.
> The common thread is not cannabis as a drug but cannabis as an ingredient: in a nasal spray, a yogurt and a mouthwash. All three are still at the bench.

A team from the Agricultural Technological Institute of Castilla y León and the University of Valladolid in Spain added an enzyme-treated hemp seed preparation to ordinary yogurt at 2%, 4% and 6%, according to the Herald's summary of the paper in Molecules. Processing the seeds more than doubled their phenolic content and raised antioxidant activity by 2.3 to 5.7 times, depending on the test.

At 2%, protein rose by about 9.7% and polyunsaturated fatty acids rose from 2.9% to 10.3% of total fatty acids. The 4% yogurt had about 4.5 times the phenolic compounds of the plain version. The researchers also measured inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme, a target of some blood-pressure drugs, in the lab: the concentration needed for inhibition fell by about 58% compared with plain yogurt. The 6% version had nearly 14 times as many lactic acid bacteria. A panel of seven trained tasters preferred the 2% and 4% versions. The Herald's headline cites antioxidant gains of up to 11-fold; the figures in its article body run to 5.7-fold for the seeds, and we have not been able to check the higher number against the paper.
Evidence level: food science and laboratory measurement. It says nothing about blood pressure in people.

Researchers from Thammasat, Mae Fah Luang and Mahidol universities in Thailand made a nanoemulsion mouthwash from full-spectrum hemp flower extract with 51.86% combined CBD and CBDA, according to the Herald's account of the paper in Dentistry Journal. They grew bacterial biofilms on 30 human enamel samples and treated them for 30 seconds twice a day for three days.

The mouthwash reduced bacterial metabolic activity by about 56% against controls and visibly disrupted the biofilm. Chlorhexidine, the standard antiseptic mouthwash, was the stronger antibacterial, but the cannabinoid formula was much less toxic to gum cells in the tests. The bacteria studied included three Streptococcus species, among them S. mutans, which is linked to tooth decay. The team also checked stability over 90 days at three temperatures.
Evidence level: laboratory study on enamel samples. No people used the mouthwash.
## What it means for the industry

For hemp and CBD businesses, these studies point to uses beyond intoxication: ingredients for food, oral care and topical or nasal products. They arrive just as the federal hemp definition tightens on 11 December, when finished products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container lose federal hemp status. A full-spectrum mouthwash or nasal product would need to meet that cap to stay in the hemp market, while hemp seed foods are generally made from seed rather than flower. Product claims based on early lab or animal work would also face scrutiny from regulators.

Watch for human trials of intranasal CBD for chronic rhinosinusitis, for consumer testing of hemp seed yogurt formulations, and for any clinical study comparing a cannabinoid mouthwash with chlorhexidine in people. Watch also for how Congress handles full-spectrum CBD in the stopgap spending bill due by 11 December.
